lessons.title: Types of Deals: Horizontal, Vertical, Conglomerate, and Reverse Mergers

children.text: A bank buying another bank, an aluminium smelter buying the company that rolls its metal into beverage cans, a tobacco company running hotels, and a profitable private firm slipping into a dormant listed shell are all called "deals". They have almost nothing else in common. Each type creates value in a different place, fails in a different way and needs a different question from you. Classify the deal first and the right questions follow.

body.text: The type of deal tells you where the synergies are supposed to come from. Horizontal deals promise scale, vertical deals promise control of the supply chain, conglomerate deals promise diversification, and reverse mergers are usually about structure. Match the promise to the type and you will spot weak stories quickly.

body.caption: The four deal types at a glance

cells: Overpaying, integration clashes, competition law hurdles
Vijaya Bank and Dena Bank into Bank of Baroda, 2019
Securing inputs or markets, capturing more of the margin chain
Taking on a business with different economics and cycles
Conglomerate discount, management spread too thin
Diversified groups later unwinding through demergers
A larger or unlisted company into a smaller or listed one
Simpler structure, a listing, or use of tax losses
Backdoor listings of weak businesses, unfair swap ratios

children.text: Horizontal Deals: Buying a Competitor

A horizontal deal combines two companies selling the same thing to the same customers. The logic is the easiest to understand: fewer players, bigger scale, overlapping branches or plants to rationalise. It is also the type most likely to attract the
Competition Commission of India
, because removing a competitor can hurt customers.

markDefs.definition: CCI, India's competition regulator. Deals above specified asset, turnover or deal-value thresholds must be notified to and approved by the CCI before they complete.

children.text: India's biggest run of horizontal deals came from the government itself. Between 2017 and 2020, it consolidated public sector banks in three waves: SBI absorbed its five associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank in April 2017, Bank of Baroda absorbed Vijaya Bank and Dena Bank in April 2019, and ten banks were merged into four in April 2020.

body.title: Convert a Vijaya Bank holding
body.prompt: Sunita held 1,500 Vijaya Bank shares on the record date. At 402 Bank of Baroda shares for every 1,000 Vijaya Bank shares, how many Bank of Baroda shares did she receive?

body.text: In a horizontal merger of equals on paper, one culture, one IT system and one set of managers usually wins. PSU bank mergers combined different core banking systems, branch networks and staff seniority lists. When you read about a horizontal deal, ask how long integration will take and who bears the disruption in the meantime.

children.text: Vertical Deals: Buying Up or Down the Supply Chain
A vertical deal joins companies at different stages of the same value chain. Buying a supplier is
backward integration
. Buying a customer or distribution channel is
forward integration

. In 2007, Hindalco, the Aditya Birla Group's aluminium producer, bought Novelis, the world's largest maker of rolled aluminium products, for about $6 billion. That moved Hindalco forward from making primary metal to making the flat-rolled sheet used in cans, cars and packaging.

markDefs.definition: Acquiring a business earlier in your supply chain, such as a tyre maker buying a rubber plantation, to secure inputs and their margin.
Acquiring a business later in your supply chain, such as a steelmaker buying a steel products fabricator or a distributor, to get closer to the end customer.

columns.label: Backward integration
points: Goal: secure raw materials and control input costs
Example pattern: a cement company buying limestone mines or a power plant
Risk: owning a commodity business with its own price cycle

columns.label: Forward integration
points: Buy a customer or distribution channel
Goal: capture more margin and get closer to the end user
Example: Hindalco buying Novelis to sell rolled products, not just metal
Risk: competing with your own former customers

body.title: Which direction?
body.question: A fictional listed tyre maker, Deccan Tyres, buys a natural rubber plantation company in Kerala that supplies about a third of its rubber. What type of deal is this?
options: Horizontal, because both companies are in the rubber business
Vertical, backward integration, because Deccan Tyres is buying its supplier
Vertical, forward integration, because the plantation sells to Deccan Tyres
Conglomerate, because farming and manufacturing are unrelated
body.explanation: The plantation sits earlier in Deccan Tyres' supply chain, so buying it is backward integration. The question for investors: does owning rubber plantations earn a better return than simply buying rubber, given that Deccan Tyres now carries the risk of rubber price swings on both sides?

children.text: Conglomerate Deals: Buying Something Unrelated

A conglomerate deal combines businesses with no real operating link. The usual justification is diversification: when one business slows, another carries the group. The problem for a listed company's shareholders is that they can diversify far more cheaply themselves. A Nifty 50 index fund gives you 50 businesses across sectors for an expense ratio well under 0.5% a year, without paying a control premium.
Markets often punish unrelated businesses under one roof with a
conglomerate discount

. That is why so many Indian groups are now doing the opposite of conglomerate deals. ITC demerged its hotels business in 2025, and Reliance demerged Jio Financial Services in 2023. Chapter 4 looks at these in detail.

markDefs.definition: The tendency of markets to value a diversified company at less than the sum of what its separate businesses would be worth on their own.

body.text: Be most sceptical when a company with a large cash pile announces an acquisition outside its core business. Spare cash that could have been returned through dividends or buybacks is being spent on a business management has never run, usually at a premium.

body.title: Name the discount
body.textWithBlank: When a diversified company trades below the combined value of its individual businesses, investors call the gap a ___ discount.
body.explanation: The conglomerate discount reflects poor capital allocation between divisions, lack of focus and limited transparency on each business. Demergers are one of the main ways Indian groups try to close it.

children.text: Reverse Mergers: When the Bigger Fish Is Absorbed
In an ordinary merger, the bigger company absorbs the smaller one. In a
reverse merger
, the roles flip. Indian investors meet the term in three situations.

markDefs.definition: A merger in which a larger, parent or unlisted company merges into a smaller, subsidiary or listed company, so the smaller or listed entity survives.

children.text: Parent into subsidiary.

The holding company merges into the operating company it controls, usually because the subsidiary holds the licence that matters. ICICI Ltd merged into its subsidiary ICICI Bank in 2002, with ICICI Ltd shareholders receiving 1 ICICI Bank share for every 2 ICICI Ltd shares. HDFC Ltd into HDFC Bank in 2023 followed the same pattern.
Profitable into loss-making.

A profitable company merges into a sister company with accumulated losses, hoping to set those losses off against future profits. Tax law allows this only when strict conditions are met, and Lesson 5.1 covers the rules.
Unlisted into listed.
A private company merges into a listed company, often a small dormant one, and gets a stock exchange listing without an IPO. This is a
backdoor listing

. Because it skips the disclosure and scrutiny of an IPO, SEBI requires such schemes to pass stock exchange review, and the listed company's existing public shareholders must not be reduced to an insignificant stake.

markDefs.definition: Getting an unlisted business listed by merging it into an already listed company, instead of going through an IPO.

body.title: Convert an ICICI Ltd holding
body.prompt: An investor held 500 ICICI Ltd shares when it merged into ICICI Bank at a ratio of 1 ICICI Bank share for every 2 ICICI Ltd shares. How many ICICI Bank shares did they receive?
body.explanation: 500 × 1 ÷ 2 = 250 ICICI Bank shares. The investor received fewer shares, but each ICICI Bank share was worth more, so the share count alone tells you nothing about gain or loss.

body.title: The shell company that hit ten upper circuits
body.scenario: A fictional BSE-listed company, Ganga Trade Links, has reported revenue under ₹1 crore for five years and trades at ₹8. It announces that a fast-growing private logistics firm will merge into it, and existing Ganga shareholders will own 5% of the combined company. The stock hits the upper circuit for ten straight sessions, and a Telegram channel says it will be "the next multibagger".
body.prompt: What kind of deal is this, and what would you check before buying?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Deal type: an unlisted-into-listed reverse merger, effectively a backdoor listing of the logistics firm.
2. Scheme and approvals: has the scheme been filed with BSE and cleared for SEBI's observations? Until the exchange and NCLT approve it, the deal may never happen.
3. The unlisted company's numbers: backdoor listings skip IPO-level disclosure. Look for audited financials, the valuation report behind the swap ratio and who owns the private firm.
4. Your dilution: existing shareholders dropping to 5% means the swap ratio decides almost everything. Check whether an independent valuer supports it.
5. Promoters and trading pattern: repeated upper circuits in a thinly traded stock with social media promotion is a classic warning pattern. Check SEBI orders and exchange surveillance measures such as ASM or GSM on the stock.
6. Liquidity: stocks locked in upper circuits often have almost no sellers on the way up and almost no buyers on the way down.

body.title: Two more labels you may see: congeneric and market extension deals

children.text: Congeneric or product extension deal.

The companies sell different but related products to the same customers, such as a company selling detergents buying a health drinks brand to push through the same grocery stores. HUL's merger with GSK Consumer Healthcare fits here.
Market extension deal.

The companies sell the same product in different geographies, such as a South India focused cement maker buying a North India focused one. It sits close to horizontal, with less overlap to cut and less competition law concern.

body.title: Classify any deal in under a minute
steps: Do the two companies sell the same product to the same customers? Horizontal
Does one supply the other, or sell what the other makes? Vertical
Is there no operating link at all? Conglomerate
Is the parent, the bigger company or the unlisted company the one being absorbed? Reverse merger
Match the type to the stated reason and check whether they agree

body.label: Competition Commission of India
body.description: The CCI publishes orders on the combinations it approves, including conditions it attaches to large horizontal deals.

cards.definition: A combination of competitors selling the same products to the same customers.
A combination of companies at different stages of the same supply chain.
Buying a supplier to secure inputs and their margin.
Buying a customer or distribution channel to get closer to the end user.
A combination of unrelated businesses, usually justified by diversification.
The gap by which a diversified company trades below the sum of its businesses' standalone values.
A merger where the larger, parent or unlisted company is absorbed into the smaller, subsidiary or listed one.
Getting an unlisted business listed by merging it into a listed company instead of doing an IPO.

points: Horizontal deals combine competitors and promise scale. India cut its public sector banks from 27 to 12 between 2017 and 2020 this way.
Vertical deals move up or down the supply chain, like Hindalco buying Novelis in 2007 to move from primary aluminium into rolled products.
Conglomerate deals combine unrelated businesses. Shareholders can diversify more cheaply themselves, and markets often apply a conglomerate discount.
Reverse mergers flip the usual roles: parent into subsidiary (ICICI Ltd into ICICI Bank), profitable into loss-making, or unlisted into listed.
Backdoor listings through small listed shells skip IPO scrutiny, so check approvals, the unlisted firm's financials and surveillance flags before getting excited.
Classify the deal first, then check whether the stated reason fits the type.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Deccan Tyres and Ganga Trade Links are fictional. Figures for real companies and banks are taken from public disclosures at the time of each deal and are rounded. Mentioning a company is not a recommendation to buy or sell its shares.
